<reason>Both sides were disciplined, format-compliant, and built genuine clash. CON's spine was a strong dilemma: teeth either fail (2015 redux) or bite only financially, at which point the quota "dissolves" into CON's own capacity-and-money alternative. That was the sharpest analytic move in the debate and it forced PRO to defend a weakened version of relocation. But PRO answered it cleanly at the decisive moment: an allocated share is what converts money from charity negotiated boat-by-boat into a debt owed to the frontline ("Greece asks" vs "Greece is owed"), so a buy-out is a mode of discharging an obligation, not a refutation of it. CON's closing restated the invoice line but never dismantled that distinction. PRO also exploited the motion's actual wording effectively: CON's alternative expressly leaves frontline states processing most arrivals, better funded. CON's reframe (the burden is throughput, not hosting) was a fair and creative answer, but it partly concedes the concentration PRO indicts and rests on the optimistic assumption that returns and adjudication speed can be fixed where they never have been. Finally, PRO's "Hungary is not Europe — a rule binding 23 states bought out by four is still a transformation" went essentially unanswered; CON continued to argue as if universal refusal were the baseline. CON's secondary-movement attack was clever but blunted by PRO's point that matching to actual destinations shifts legal and fiscal responsibility to the receiving state, which CON dismissed rather than refuted. Narrow but real edge to PRO on weighing and on resolving the central dilemma.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's answer to CON's dissolution dilemma: a quota with a buy-out is "an obligation with two ways of discharging it" — delete the quota and the money becomes charity, keep it and the money becomes a debt. That reframe neutralized CON's strongest structural attack while turning CON's own capacity-fund alternative into evidence for the motion.</best_rebuttal>
